## Abstract

`jmjax` fits joint longitudinal-survival models with NUTS/HMC. This
document concerns two features of the joint model's posterior geometry
that decide how fast a sampler mixes. The first is an obstacle every
hierarchical regression shares, which a reparameterization removes. The
second is intrinsic to joint models: it decides how fast a sampler can
mix the association parameter, and it favours NUTS over blocked samplers
by construction.

The first is a *location degeneracy*. The likelihood pins the
sum of a subject-constant fixed effect and the matching linear combination
of the random effects, but not the split between them. Section 3 names the
mechanism and traces it to source, including a finding that is easy to
miss. The same degeneracy recurs between the fixed slope on time and the
mean random slope, for any model with a random slope, whatever the number
of covariates.

Section 4 characterizes exactly which random-effect directions are
absorbable, defining them jointly across random-effect columns (a shift of
the fixed effects may have to be offset in several at once), gives a
construction that depends only on the column space of the fixed-effects
design, and states the condition the survival submodel imposes. Section 5 uses that basis
for an exact rotation (`control$rotate_absorbable`). Every random-effect
column is rotated by one fixed orthogonal matrix, so the absorbable
directions become an explicit, small block of sampling coordinates. The
fixed effects and that block then get a single small dense mass-matrix
block (`control$dense_mass_generator_beta`). The rotation changes no
prior, no likelihood and no reported quantity: it only changes which
coordinates NUTS adapts to.

In simulation (Section 6), across ten designs, the rotation raises the
effective sample size per second (ESS/sec) of the regression coefficients
a user reports by 8x-25x for the intercept and 8x-60x for the time slope
(geometric means 14x and 21x), at the same wall time. Coverage in a
100-replicate calibration study agrees with the unrotated fit's within
Monte Carlo error. On two real datasets (Section 7), the intercept and
subject-constant covariates gain 17x-28x and the time slope 2.3x-4.4x.
For random-intercept-only models the gains on the intercept and
subject-constant covariates are 19x-53x on the same data, and in
simulation the unrotated fit often failed to converge at the standard run
length where the rotated one did (Section 5.3). Section 8 compares with
`JMbayes2`. With the rotation, `jmjax` matches it on the coefficients
`JMbayes2` hierarchically centres, where the unrotated fit trailed by a
factor of 17-33, and leads on the rest.

The second finding concerns the association parameter `alpha`, which
measures how the longitudinal marker relates to the hazard. Studying that
association is the reason to fit a joint model at all, so `alpha` is the
parameter a joint-model analysis is chiefly run to estimate and draw
inferences about. `jmjax` mixes it 3x-8x faster than `JMbayes2` with no
option enabled, and 7x-8x faster on real data with the rotation.

- **Why (Proposition 8).** Consider a sampler that updates `alpha`
  conditional on the other parameters. Its lag-1 autocorrelation for
  `alpha` is the fraction of `alpha`'s posterior variance those
  parameters explain, $R^2$, so its cost grows like $1/(1-R^2)$. HMC moves
  `alpha` together with the rest. It pays only in integration steps, which
  grow at most like $1/\sqrt{1-R^2}$, and often not at all.
- **How large $R^2$ is.** On `aids` and `pbc2`, 0.87 and 0.85 of
  `alpha`'s posterior variance is shared with the other parameters.
  Almost all of it is shared with the survival block: `alpha` trades off
  against the level of the log hazard. The random effects account for
  much less. So even an ideal blocked sampler, drawing each full
  conditional exactly, would keep at most one effective draw in 13-15.
- **How much of the gap it explains.** On a log scale, that structural
  limit accounts for about three quarters of `jmjax`'s ESS-per-draw
  advantage over `JMbayes2` on `alpha` (73%-78%). The rest is a
  difference between the two transition kernels that this comparison does
  not decompose further (Section 8.1).

This advantage is a property of the joint model and of how the sampler
updates it, not of any `jmjax` option. It is generic to gradient
samplers that move all parameters together.

A stress grid of the designs the theory predicts are hardest for the
rotation keeps the gains at 5x-30x (Section 6.4). On the strength of these
checks, the rotation is `jmjax`'s default wherever it applies,
including random-intercept-only models. Throughout this document, "the
unrotated fit" is the parameterization it replaced, still available as
`rotate_absorbable = FALSE`.

An earlier approach, which swept the absorbable directions out of the
random effects instead of rotating them, is retired. It is documented in
the package repository's development record
(`dev/notes/sweep-reparameterization.md`).


## 1. Motivation

Across every real and simulated dataset `jmjax` has been benchmarked on, its
NUTS/HMC sampler mixes better than `JMbayes2`'s sampler - sometimes by a
modest, explainable margin, sometimes by a striking one. Two different
things contribute, and they should not be conflated. One is generic: a
gradient-based sampler that moves all parameters jointly is not slowed by
inter-block correlation the way a block-Gibbs sampler is (Sections 2.4,
8). The other is specific to this model class: a location degeneracy
between fixed and random effects that slows *any* sampler on the
regression coefficients, including `jmjax`'s own unrotated fit, and that a
targeted reparameterization can remove (Sections 3-6).

One parameter deserves to be singled out from the start. A joint model
exists to estimate the *association* between the longitudinal process and
the event hazard: `alpha`, the log hazard ratio per unit of the current
underlying marker value. Treatment effects on the marker, its trajectory
over time and the baseline hazard matter, but they could be studied with
separate models. The association cannot. So when this document compares
samplers, the question that matters most is how well each one estimates
`alpha`. That question comes back in Section 8.1, which also gives a
theoretical account of why NUTS has the advantage there.

This is worth writing up carefully rather than reporting only headline
ratios. The mechanism is real, reproducible, and - as far as a literature
search turned up - not previously documented in exactly this form for
joint models (Section 2.6). And an honest accounting has to say which part
of the advantage belongs to which cause.

## 2. Background: reparameterization in hierarchical Bayesian models

### 2.1 Centered and non-centered parameterizations

The general problem of how a hierarchical model's *parameterization* -
independent of its likelihood - determines whether a given MCMC sampler
mixes well is the subject of a substantial literature going back at least to
Papaspiliopoulos & Roberts (2003), "Non-Centered Parameterisations for
Hierarchical Models and Data Augmentation," in *Bayesian Statistics 7*
(Bernardo et al., eds., Oxford University Press), and formalized in
Papaspiliopoulos, Roberts & Sköld (2007), "A General Framework for the
Parametrization of Hierarchical Models," *Statistical Science*, 22(1),
59-73 (also arXiv:0708.3797). Their central point, restated for this
setting: whether a hierarchical parameter should be sampled in its "centered"
form (as the quantity of direct scientific interest) or a "non-centered"
form (as a standardized deviation from a mean, with the mean itself a
separate parameter) is not a matter of taste - it changes which directions
of the posterior a given sampler can move efficiently along, and the right
choice depends on how informative the data are relative to the prior for
that parameter.

### 2.2 Why this bites gradient-based samplers specifically

Betancourt & Girolami (2013), "Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Hierarchical
Models" (arXiv:1312.0906), and Betancourt (2017), "A Conceptual
Introduction to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo" (arXiv:1701.02434), give the
geometric account of *why* a poor parameterization specifically hurts
Hamiltonian/NUTS samplers: HMC's efficiency depends on a roughly uniform
curvature (so a single, global step size and mass matrix work everywhere),
and a degenerate or near-degenerate direction in the posterior - a ridge, or
a funnel - forces the sampler either to take very small steps (to stay
stable along the narrow direction) or to fail to move efficiently along the
wide one. Hoffman & Gelman (2014), "The No-U-Turn Sampler," *Journal of
Machine Learning Research*, 15, 1593-1623, is the reference for NUTS itself
and documents the same general sensitivity to posterior geometry that
motivates adaptive path-length selection in the first place.

**Neal's funnel is a different pathology and should not be conflated with
this one.** The canonical hard case for HMC in hierarchical models, due to
Neal (2003), "Slice Sampling," *Annals of Statistics*, 31(3), 705-767, is a
*curvature* problem: a hierarchical variance parameter changes the scale of
the parameters below it, so the posterior narrows sharply in one region and
widens in another, and no single step size handles both. The location
degeneracy this document is about is not a curvature problem - the
posterior's curvature along the degenerate direction is essentially flat
(it is informed only by a prior, not sharpened or narrowed by the
likelihood at all). Both problems are usefully addressed by
reparameterization, and both are discussed together in introductions to HMC
for exactly that reason, but they are mechanistically distinct and the fix
for one is not automatically evidence for, or against, the other.

### 2.3 A directly analogous, already-quantified example

Stan's own User's Guide, in its "Collinearity" / redundant-intercepts
discussion of "Problematic Posteriors," works through almost exactly the
degeneracy this document is about: a model with two intercept parameters
whose likelihood is invariant to adding a constant to one and subtracting it
from the other, so only their *sum* is identified. Stan's documented,
measured comparison (100 data points, standard normal) across three
versions of that model is close enough to `jmjax`'s own case to quote
directly:

| Model | Mean leapfrog steps | ESS/sec | R-hat |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Non-identified (flat prior on both intercepts) | ~1,400 | ~200 | 5.2 (non-convergent) |
| Weakly identified (both intercepts given a `normal(0, 10)` prior) | ~150 | ~1,900 | 1.0 |
| Identified (single intercept) | ~3 | ~31,000 | 1.0 |

The "weakly identified" row is the mechanistically exact analogue of
`jmjax`'s unrotated fit: `jmjax` does not leave `beta_0`
and `mean(b_i0)` entirely unconstrained (that would be improper), it
constrains their *split* only through the prior on the random effects, at
scale `sigma_b0/sqrt(N)` - a weak, N-dependent identifying prior in
precisely the sense of Stan's middle row. Reading the ratios off that row
relative to the fully identified one - roughly 50x more leapfrog steps and
roughly 16x lower ESS/sec from the *weak-prior* case alone, before even
reaching the fully non-identified case - is a useful, independently-sourced
sanity check on the magnitude of what a location degeneracy costs, prior to
any numbers specific to `jmjax` below.

### 2.4 The other side: why block/conditional samplers are specifically vulnerable

Roberts & Sahu (1997), "Updating Schemes, Correlation Structure, Blocking
and Parameterization for the Gibbs Sampler," *Journal of the Royal
Statistical Society, Series B*, 59(2), 291-317, is the classical reference
for the complementary fact this document needs for Section 8: a Gibbs
sampler that updates parameters in blocks (as `JMbayes2`'s does - it
combines Metropolis-within-Gibbs updates for regression coefficients with a
closed-form conditional update for the random-effects covariance) degrades
specifically as the *correlation between blocks* grows, because each block
is updated conditional on the current value of the others and can only move
as fast as that conditional distribution allows. This is a distinct
mechanism from the location degeneracy itself: it does not require an
unidentified direction, only a strongly correlated one, and it predicts
degradation that tracks *inter-block correlation growing with problem size*
even in a model that is *fully* identified everywhere - which is exactly
the shape of the `JMbayes2` covariance-collapse finding in Section 8.2.

### 2.5 Applied precedent

Ogle et al. (2020), "Ensuring Identifiability in Hierarchical Mixed Effects
Bayesian Models," *Ecological Applications*, 30(7), e02159, documents the
same class of problem (fixed effects and random effects competing to
explain the same variation) arising in applied hierarchical models outside
the joint-modeling literature, and is useful as evidence that this is a
recognized, recurring failure mode across the wider Bayesian hierarchical-
modeling literature rather than an artifact specific to joint models.

### 2.6 What appears to be genuinely new here

A deliberately honest gap: no prior work was found that documents this
*exact* instance - a random-slope-mean-vs-fixed-slope-coefficient aliasing,
in a *joint* longitudinal-survival model, empirically shown to explain a
*widening* efficiency disadvantage for a competing block-sampler
implementation as covariate count grows, with the covariate-count-
independence of the underlying mechanism itself confirmed against the
sampler's own source code. The pieces above (non-centered reparameterization
theory, HMC's specific sensitivity to it, Gibbs samplers' specific
sensitivity to growing correlation) are all separately well established;
their combination and application to this specific model class, with this
specific empirical signature, is offered here as this document's actual
contribution - not a rediscovery of general theory.

### 2.7 A related point this document needed later: ESS is a property of the functional, not the sampler

Geyer (1992), "Practical Markov Chain Monte Carlo," *Statistical Science*,
7(4), 473-483, is the classical reference for a fact that becomes
load-bearing in Sections 5 and 6: effective sample size and Monte Carlo standard
error are defined with respect to a *specific scalar function* of the
chain being averaged, not as a property of the sampler or the state vector
in the abstract. Two different linear functionals of the same joint draws
- say, a sampled coordinate, and a different linear combination of that
coordinate with another block entirely - can therefore have arbitrarily
different effective sample sizes even though they come from the identical
run. This is not a surprising or unusual fact in the MCMC literature; it
is why Section 6 measures ESS on the coefficients a user reports, not on
whatever coordinates the sampler happens to use internally.

## 3. The location degeneracy in jmjax's joint model

### 3.1 Setup

`jmjax`'s longitudinal submodel, for the random-intercept-and-slope case
(`random_effects = "intercept_slope"`, `q = 2`) that this document is
concerned with, is

$$y_{ij} = \beta^\top x_{ij} + b_{i0} + b_{i1} t_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}$$

with `beta` the fixed-effects vector (including an intercept and any
baseline covariates), `b_i = (b_{i0}, b_{i1})` subject-level random effects
with a correlated Normal prior, and `t_ij` the time of observation `j` for
subject `i`. The survival submodel links to this through `alpha` and the
usual functional forms; nothing below changes as a function of the survival
side, so it is suppressed in this section's notation.

### 3.2 The intercept-level degeneracy (established prior to this document)

If `x_ij` contains an intercept column (or, more generally, any column that
is constant within subject `i`), a shift `b_{i0} -> b_{i0} + s_i` for a
subject-constant `s_i` changes nothing about the fitted mean as long as
`beta` absorbs the matching shift on that column - the likelihood
constrains only the **sum**, not the individual split. This was already
diagnosed and documented (`vignette("jmjax-validation")`, "The experimental
`wishart_gibbs_centered` option"; see also the `orthogonalize_b0`
documentation in `?jm_fit`) prior to the work in this document, via a
measured `corr(beta_0, mean(b_i0)) ~= -0.95` on real data and the resulting
poor `beta_0` mixing.

**An earlier attempted fix, and why it was retracted.**
`control$random_effects_method = "wishart_gibbs_centered"` addressed this
by constraining the random intercepts to sum to exactly zero at *every*
posterior draw - a hard, exact Gibbs-sampler constraint. It worked, in the
narrow sense of improving `beta_0`'s mixing (`beta_0` ESS improved roughly
4.8x in its own validation). But further validation at a larger sample size
found it introduces a genuine, quantitatively characterized **credible-
interval miscalibration** for `beta_0`: point estimates stayed unbiased, but
the reported posterior standard deviation did not fully reflect the true
uncertainty, because the exact constraint removes real finite-sample
variability in the sample mean of the true random intercepts that `beta_0`
must otherwise absorb. It is documented in the package as exploratory only,
not recommended for final inference. This episode matters for what follows
in two ways: it establishes that this general class of problem is not
solved just by "removing" the degeneracy by any means available, and it is
the point of comparison Section 3.4 returns to.

### 3.3 The same degeneracy recurs for the random slope, independently of covariate count

The intercept-level degeneracy grows with the number of subject-constant
covariates, since each adds one absorbable direction. A second degeneracy
does not grow with them at all. It lies between the fixed slope on `time`,
`beta_1`, and the population *mean* of the random slopes, `mean(b_i1)`, and
it is present as soon as there is any random slope on time. `jmjax`'s
basis construction finds it from the design matrices rather than assuming
it. The docstring of `_absorbable_basis` (`inst/python/jmjax_backend/absorbable.py`)
states it plainly:

> "For q = 1 (a random slope on time) it picks up `time` itself, giving the
> sum-to-zero constraint on b_1, and would also pick up any
> covariate-by-time interaction present in X."

Whenever the fixed-effects design includes a `time` column and there is a
correlated random slope on time, the fixed slope and the mean random slope
are aliased in exactly the same "sum is identified, split is not" sense as
the intercept case. This holds with no extra covariates just as much as
with twelve. It shows up directly in the measurements. In a replicated
covariate-count sweep (k = 1, 4, 8, 12; recorded in the development record,
Section 6), the binding - lowest-ESS - regression parameter under the
unrotated fit was `beta_1` at every `k`, never one of the covariate
coefficients. In Section 6's grid, the unrotated fit's time slope mixes
slowest of the three monitored parameters in 7 of the 10 cells.

### 3.4 Addressing it: rotate, don't constrain

There are two obvious ways to deal with a degeneracy of this kind. One is
to remove it: constrain or project the random effects so the absorbable
directions are no longer free. `jmjax` tried this twice. An exact
sum-to-zero Gibbs constraint (`wishart_gibbs_centered`, Section 3.2)
miscalibrated `beta_0`'s intervals. A NUTS-space projection
(`orthogonalize_b0`/`orthogonalize_b`) did the same until an exact
correction was derived, after which its reportable efficiency gain was
modest. Both are retired; the second is documented in full in the
development record. The other way leaves the model and its coordinates'
meaning alone, and changes only which coordinates the sampler adapts to.
That is what `jmjax` does (Section 5). Section 4 characterizes the
directions involved, since the rotation needs a basis for them.

### 3.5 Previously-measured magnitude, real data

The package documentation for the retired sweep option (`?jm_fit`,
`orthogonalize_b0`) recorded a direct measurement on the `pbc2` dataset
(n = 312, 4 chains x 1000 draws, figures reported in the space NUTS actually
samples): with an intercept and one baseline covariate in the design,

- `corr(beta_0, mean(b_i0)) = -0.9709`
- `corr(beta_2, age-slope(b_i0)) = -0.9715`
- against `+0.0543` for `beta_1` (a within-subject, non-absorbable
  contrast, included as a negative control)
- minimum ESS for the two affected coefficients alone, 441 and 526, against
  2893 and >4000 for the corresponding *identified sums* - a recoverable
  factor of **6.6x and >7.6x**.

## 4. The absorbable directions: definition, characterization, construction

The rotation of Section 5 is exact for *any* fixed orthogonal matrix. What
the basis controls is whether the rotation does anything useful. It should
contain every absorbable direction (completeness), so that none is left
spread across the per-subject coordinates. And it should contain only
absorbable directions (soundness), so that it does not spend the explicit
block on directions the data already pin down. A shift of the fixed effects
may have to be offset in several random-effect columns at once, so the
directions are defined jointly across columns. This section gives the
definition, its characterization, the condition the survival submodel adds,
two designs where checking one column at a time misses directions, and the
construction `jmjax` uses from version 0.4.0. It follows Section 3 of the
methods paper.

### 4.1 Notation

Index subjects by $i = 1, \dots, N$ and subject $i$'s longitudinal
observations by $j = 1, \dots, n_i$, taken at times $t_{ij}$. Write
$X_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n_i \times p}$ for subject $i$'s fixed-effects design
and $Z_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n_i \times q}$ for its random-effects design, and
$x_i(t)$, $z_i(t)$ for the design rows at time $t$. Let
$B \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times q}$ collect the random effects, with rows
$b_i^{\top}$, and $\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$ the fixed effects.

The random effects enter the joint likelihood in exactly two ways: through
the longitudinal mean $\mu_{ij} = x_{ij}^{\top}\beta + z_{ij}^{\top} b_i$,
and through the shared trajectory $m_i(t) = x_i(t)^{\top}\beta +
z_i(t)^{\top} b_i$, which enters the hazard through $\alpha$ and is
evaluated at the event time $T_i$ and at the Gauss-Legendre quadrature
nodes used for the cumulative hazard (and, with a `delta`, `area` or
`area_avg` association, through the corresponding transforms of
$m_i$). The second channel is easy to overlook: `X_long` and `Z_long` are
not the only arrays through which `b` reaches the likelihood, since
`X_time_surv`/`Z_time_surv` and `X_time_quad`/`Z_time_quad` carry it too.
All of them are built from the *same* `long_formula` and `random_formula`,
evaluated at different times with the subject's baseline covariates.

### 4.2 What "absorbable" means

**Definition 1 (invariant shift; absorbable subspace).** A pair
$(d, \Delta)$, with $d \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$ and $\Delta \in
\mathbb{R}^{N \times q}$ with rows $\delta_i^{\top}$, is an *invariant
shift* if $\beta \mapsto \beta + d$, $B \mapsto B + \Delta$ leaves every
longitudinal mean and every trajectory, and hence the likelihood,
unchanged:

$$X_i\, d + Z_i\, \delta_i = 0 \qquad \text{for every } i, \tag{L}$$

$$x_i(t)^{\top} d + z_i(t)^{\top} \delta_i = 0
\qquad \text{for every } i \text{ and every } t \in [0, \tau]. \tag{T}$$

In a mixed model without a survival submodel, (L) is the whole requirement.
A shift with $d = 0$ is *null*: then $\delta_i \in K_i$, where
$K_i = \ker Z_i$ in a mixed model and
$K_i = \{a : z_i(t)^{\top} a = 0 \text{ for all } t \in [0, \tau]\}$ in a
joint model. For each *witness* $d$ (a $d$ for which some invariant shift
exists), let $\Delta(d)$ be the invariant shift whose rows are orthogonal
to the $K_i$; it is unique, because two solutions for subject $i$ differ by
an element of $K_i$. The *absorbable subspace*
$\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{N}$ is the span of the columns of
$\Delta(d)$ over all witnesses $d$.

Three remarks fix the scope. First, invariance of $\mu$ and $m$ implies
invariance of the whole joint likelihood, so the definition is about
*likelihood* invariance. It is emphatically not about the prior: the prior
on $b$ is not invariant under these shifts, and that asymmetry is what
pins the split at all (Section 4.7). Second, a null shift moves only
random-effect coordinates the likelihood never sees, such as the slope of
a subject observed only at baseline in a mixed model. The prior alone sets
their scale and they involve no fixed effect, so they create no ridge and
need no treatment. Third, the likelihood uses $m_i(t)$ only up to each
subject's event or censoring time, so requiring (T) on all of $[0, \tau]$
is slightly more than likelihood invariance needs. It makes $\mathcal{A}$
a structural property of the model rather than of the observed follow-up.

Up to version 0.3.x, `jmjax` defined absorbable directions one
random-effect column at a time: a vector $v$ for column $c$, with
$X_i d = -v_i\, Z_i e_c$. That is the special case of Definition 1 in which
$\Delta$ is nonzero in a single column, and Section 4.5 shows it can miss
directions.

### 4.3 Exact characterization

Let $P_{Z_i} = Z_i Z_i^{+}$ be the orthogonal projector onto the range of
$Z_i$, with $Z_i^{+}$ the Moore-Penrose inverse, and let
$M \in \mathbb{R}^{(\sum_i n_i) \times p}$ stack the matrices
$(I - P_{Z_i}) X_i$.

**Proposition 1 (characterization).** In a mixed model, $d$ is a witness
if and only if $d \in \ker M$, and then $\delta_i(d) = -Z_i^{+} X_i d$ for
every $i$. Hence $\mathcal{A}$ is spanned by the columns of $\Delta(d)$ for
$d$ in any basis of $\ker M$, $\dim \mathcal{A} \le q \dim \ker M \le qp$,
and $\mathcal{A}$ depends on the fixed-effects design only through its
column space.

*Proof.* Equation (L) has a solution $\delta_i$ if and only if
$X_i d \in \operatorname{range} Z_i$, that is, $(I - P_{Z_i}) X_i d = 0$.
Its solutions are $-Z_i^{+} X_i d + \ker Z_i$, and $Z_i^{+}$ maps into
$(\ker Z_i)^{\perp}$, so $-Z_i^{+} X_i d$ is the one orthogonal to
$K_i = \ker Z_i$. Replacing $X$ by $XG$ with $G$ invertible maps $\ker M$
to $G^{-1}\ker M$ and leaves each $X_i d$, hence each $\Delta(d)$,
unchanged. $\square$

So one singular value decomposition of $M$ gives a basis of $\ker M$; each
basis vector $d$ gives an $N \times q$ matrix $\Delta(d)$; and a second
decomposition of the $N \times (q \dim \ker M)$ matrix of their columns
gives an orthonormal basis $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times k}$ of
$\mathcal{A}$.

### 4.4 The survival submodel: Condition (S)

In a joint model, requirement (T) quantifies over all $t \in [0, \tau]$,
while $M$ sees only the observation times.

**Condition (S) - structural extension.** For every $d \in \ker M$ and
every subject $i$, the function $t \mapsto x_i(t)^{\top} d$ on
$[0, \tau]$ is a linear combination of the random-effect basis functions
$t \mapsto z_i(t)^{\top} e_c$, $c = 1, \dots, q$; that is, (T) has a
solution $\delta_i$.

**Proposition 2 (joint model).** In a joint model every witness lies in
$\ker M$; under (S) the witnesses are exactly $\ker M$, and $\delta_i(d)$
is the solution of (T) orthogonal to $K_i$. If $Z_i$ has full column rank,
$\delta_i(d) = -Z_i^{+} X_i d$, as in a mixed model. If it does not,
$\delta_i(d)$ is fixed by (T) and in general is not the minimum-norm
solution of (L).

*Proof.* The observation rows are $x_i(t_{ij})^{\top}$ and
$z_i(t_{ij})^{\top}$, so (T) implies (L) and every witness lies in
$\ker M$; (S) gives the converse. Two solutions of (T) differ by an element
of $K_i$, so the one orthogonal to $K_i$ is unique. If $Z_i$ has full
column rank, (L) has the single solution $-Z_i^{+} X_i d$, which every
solution of (T) satisfies. $\square$

(S) holds for subject-constant columns (absorbed by the intercept,
$z_i(t) \equiv 1$), the time column (absorbed by a random slope),
covariate-by-time interactions, and combinations of them: in each,
$x_i(t)^{\top} d$ is a combination of $1$ and $t$ as a function of $t$,
not by coincidence at the observed times. For a polynomial random-effect
basis such as $(1, t)$, $K_i = \{0\}$, so the survival submodel pins every
coordinate, including those the longitudinal data leave free (Section 4.6).

**Proposition 3 (a sufficient condition).** Suppose that, for subject $i$
and every $d \in \ker M$, the function
$t \mapsto x_i(t)^{\top} d + z_i(t)^{\top} \delta_i$, with $\delta_i$ the
solution of (L) orthogonal to $\ker Z_i$, lies in a linear space of
functions of dimension at most the number of distinct observation times of
subject $i$ that contains no nonzero function vanishing at all of them
(polynomials of degree below that number, for instance). Then (S) holds for
subject $i$.

*Proof.* The function vanishes at every observation time by (L), and the
only such function in the space is zero. $\square$

(S) can fail for spline bases in time with few observations per subject,
where a relation may hold at the observed points by coincidence. It is
cheap to check, and `jmjax` checks it at every fit (Section 4.8).

### 4.5 Designs where one-at-a-time checks fail

Two natural shortcuts each find a subspace of $\mathcal{A}$, but not always
all of it. The first looks for columns of $X$ that are *individually*
subject-constant multiples of a random-effect column. An early
development version of `jmjax` used it.

**Example 1 (a spline or orthogonal-polynomial longitudinal mean).** Let
every subject be observed at the same $m \geq 3$ distinct times, let
$Z_i = [\,1,\ t\,]$, and let

$$X_i = [\,1,\ \ t + \tfrac{1}{2}t^{2},\ \ t^{2}\,].$$

The ratios of the three columns of $X_i$ to $t$ are $1/t$,
$1 + \tfrac12 t$ and $t$, none constant, so a search over the columns of
$X$ finds no slope direction. Yet $d = (0, 1, -\tfrac12)$ gives
$X_i d = t$ and $\Delta(d) = [\,\mathbf{0},\ -\mathbf{1}_N\,]$, an
absorbable direction in the slope column.

The example is not contrived. Its column space is
$\operatorname{span}\{1, t, t^2\}$, exactly what `y ~ poly(time, 2)` or a
natural-spline longitudinal mean produces. The raw monomial spelling
`y ~ time + I(time^2)` is caught, because there `time` appears as its own
column. With the column search, the $\beta_1 \leftrightarrow
\overline{b_{i1}}$ degeneracy of Section 3.3 went untreated, and silently,
because the intercept column still yielded a basis.

The second shortcut asks, one random-effect column at a time, which shifts
of that column alone the fixed effects can absorb (a null-space
computation over the column space of $X$, so it handles Example 1), and
takes the union of the resulting spaces. `jmjax` used it in versions 0.3.x
(`_absorbable_basis_exact()`).

**Example 2 (a coupled shift).** Let $Z_i = [\,1,\ t\,]$, let every
subject have at least two distinct observation times, and let
$X_i = [\,1,\ t,\ x_i(1 + t)\,]$ for a nonconstant subject covariate
$x_i$. A shift confined to the intercept column needs $X_i d$ constant in
$t$, which forces $d \propto e_1$; one confined to the slope column needs
$X_i d \propto t$, which forces $d \propto e_2$. Both give only
$\mathbf{1}_N$. But $d = e_3$ is a witness with
$\delta_i(d) = (-x_i, -x_i)$, so
$\mathcal{A} = \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{1}, x\}$: the shift
$\beta_x \mapsto \beta_x + c$, $b_{i0} \mapsto b_{i0} - c\,x_i$,
$b_{i1} \mapsto b_{i1} - c\,x_i$ leaves every trajectory unchanged but is
invisible column by column.

**Proposition 4 (when the shortcuts are enough).** Suppose every column of
$X$ is a subject-constant covariate times one random-effect basis function
(an intercept, time, subject-constant covariates and their interactions
with time), and each subject's shift is unique ($Z_i$ of full column rank,
or $K_i = \{0\}$ in a joint model). Then $\ker M = \mathbb{R}^{p}$, each
$\Delta(e_j)$ is nonzero only in the column of that basis function, and
$\mathcal{A}$ is the union of the column-by-column spaces.

*Proof.* Each $X_i e_j$ is a subject-constant multiple of one column of
$Z_i$, so it lies in the range of $Z_i$, and $\delta_i(e_j)$ is that
multiple, with a minus sign, in that column. $\square$

All the designs of Sections 5-8, and both designs of the methods paper's
Section 7, are of this kind.

### 4.6 Subjects whose own data do not determine their shift

When $Z_i$ is rank-deficient on subject $i$'s observation rows, (L) leaves
part of $\delta_i$ free. The typical case is a subject observed only at
baseline: with $Z_i = (1, 0)$, the slope entry does not appear in (L) at
all.

**Proposition 5.** In a joint model with $K_i = \{0\}$ (for example a
polynomial random-effect basis), $\delta_i(d)$ is determined by (T) for
every subject, including those whose observation rows leave it free, and
it can differ from the minimum-norm solution of (L).

*Proof.* Immediate from Proposition 2. For a baseline-only subject and
$d = e_{\text{time}}$: the minimum-norm solution of (L) is $(0, 0)$, while
(T) requires $t + \delta_{i1} t = 0$ for all $t$, so
$\delta_i = (0, -1)$. $\square$

So a baseline-only subject's slope entry is not free in the joint model:
the survival submodel sees the subject's trajectory at its event time and
quadrature nodes, and that pins it. Using the minimum-norm longitudinal
solution, which can leave it at zero, gives a direction the likelihood does
identify.

Versions 0.3.x handled this subject by subject: a subject whose own data
did not determine its ratio took the median of the determined subjects'
ratios. That is right for uniform directions (the constant, `time`), where
(T) forces the common value, and it fixed the earlier fallback of zero,
which had left $\overline{b_{i1}}$ untreated
(`dev/diag_slope_projection.R`). But it is wrong for a covariate-weighted
direction, such as the one a `x:time` column gives a random slope: there
(T) forces $x_i$, not the median, and the per-column construction admitted
a direction that is not absorbable. The rotation stayed exact (any fixed
rotation is), but the explicit block held a direction the data identify.
From 0.4.0, (T) is solved directly.

### 4.7 What this establishes

**Corollary 1 (model invariance).** Let $(d, \Delta)$ be an invariant
shift. Then for any parameter values, replacing $(\beta, B)$ by
$(\beta + c\,d,\; B + c\,\Delta)$ leaves $\mu_{ij}$, $m_i(t)$, the hazard,
and hence the entire joint likelihood exactly unchanged.

Corollary 1 is the precise sense in which the degeneracy is a degeneracy:
along an invariant shift the likelihood is exactly flat. Nothing here
involves the prior. The prior on the random effects is *not* invariant
under these shifts, and that asymmetry is what pins the split at all (at
scale $\sigma_b/\sqrt{N}$ for the intercept's mean direction).

### 4.8 What the implementation does

From version 0.4.0 the rotation is built by `_absorbable_basis_joint()`
(`inst/python/jmjax_backend/absorbable.py`), once, before sampling:

1. **$\ker M$.** One SVD of the stacked $(I - P_{Z_i}) X_i$, with the
   columns of $X$ scaled to unit norm so that the rank decision is
   unit-free.
2. **$\Delta(d)$ from (T).** For each basis vector $d$, $\delta_i(d)$ is
   the pseudoinverse solution of (T) on subject $i$'s grid: the observation
   times, the event time, the quadrature nodes and any `delta`/`area`/
   `area_avg` rows the hazard uses. That is the solution orthogonal to
   the grid's null space of $Z_i$, which is $K_i$ (Proposition 2) for any
   polynomial random-effect basis such as `~ 1` or `~ time`. With a
   random-effect basis that vanishes on part of a subject's range (a
   spline with a knot beyond the subject's event time), the grid leaves
   that coordinate free where Definition 1, on $[0, \tau]$, would pin it,
   and the two can differ.
3. **Condition (S), checked and enforced.** The worst relative residual of
   (T) over a basis of $\ker M$ is recorded. If it exceeds $10^{-6}$, the
   fit warns, and only the subspace of $\ker M$ on which (T) holds is
   admitted, so a direction that fails (S) is never rotated.
4. **Verification.** Every admitted generator $(d, \Delta(d))$ is checked
   against (L) and (T) before use, so a loose rank tolerance cannot admit a
   direction that is not absorbable.
5. **$Q$.** One SVD of the $N \times (q \dim \ker M)$ matrix of the
   (normalized) columns of the $\Delta(d)$.

It costs about 0.2 seconds at $N = 8000$. What it did is reported in
`fit$convergence$orthogonalize$rotation`: `k`, `dim_ker_M`,
`condition_s_residual`, `n_rejected_condition_s`, and, for comparison, the
0.3.x per-column construction's dimension (`k_columnwise`) and the
distance between the two subspaces (`columnwise_subspace_distance`, the
sine of the largest principal angle).

`tests/testthat/python/check_joint_construction.py` checks the
construction against the reference implementation of the methods paper:
Examples 1 and 2, a baseline-only subject, a rank-deficient $Z_i$, a design
where (S) fails, $q = 3$, invariance under $X \mapsto XG$, and 80
randomized designs. `dev/verify_joint_vs_columnwise.R` reads the
comparison fields off fits of the designs of Sections 5-8. By
Proposition 4 they must agree there, so the numbers reported in this
document, which used the 0.3.x construction, do not depend on the change.
(The orthonormal basis chosen inside the same subspace can differ, so a
rerun under 0.4.0 does not reproduce 0.3.x draws bit for bit.)

## 5. The rotation

### 5.1 Construction and exactness

The random effects are sampled non-centred:
$b = b_{\mathrm{std}} L^{\top}$, with the entries of
$b_{\mathrm{std}} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times q}$ independent $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$
a priori and $L = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_b) L_{\mathrm{corr}}$
lower-triangular; write $\theta$ for every other parameter, including
$\beta$, $\sigma_b$ and $L_{\mathrm{corr}}$. Let $Q_{\cup} \in
\mathbb{R}^{N \times k}$ be an orthonormal basis of the absorbable
subspace $\mathcal{A}$ (Section 4). (The subscript is historical: up to
0.3.x it was the union of per-column bases.)
Complete $Q_{\cup}$ to an orthogonal matrix $R = [\,Q_{\cup} \mid
Q_{\perp}\,]$. `jmjax` uses the Householder completion, stored as $k$
reflectors, so it costs $O(Nk)$ memory and work and needs no seed.

**Proposition 6 (fixed rotations are exact).** Let
$R = [\,Q_{\cup} \mid Q_{\perp}\,]$ be any fixed $N \times N$ orthogonal
matrix, and $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \{0, \dots, q-1\}$ any set of columns.
Reparameterize $b_{\mathrm{std}}[\,\cdot\,, j] = Q_{\cup} U[\,\cdot\,, j]
+ Q_{\perp} V[\,\cdot\,, j]$ for $j \in \mathcal{C}$ (other columns
unchanged), with independent $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ priors on the entries of
$U \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times \lvert\mathcal{C}\rvert}$ and
$V \in \mathbb{R}^{(N-k) \times \lvert\mathcal{C}\rvert}$.
Then (i) the map $(U, V) \mapsto b_{\mathrm{std}}$ is linear with
$\lvert\det\rvert = 1$; (ii) the prior it induces on $b_{\mathrm{std}}$ is
exactly the original one; (iii) consequently the posterior of every model
quantity - $b$ and $\theta$ - is identical to the unrotated parameterization's, and so is every
calibration property of every estimand, up to Monte Carlo error; and (iv)
$U[\,\cdot\,, j] = Q_{\cup}^{\top} b_{\mathrm{std}}[\,\cdot\,, j]$.

*Proof.* On each rotated column the map is multiplication by the
orthogonal $R$, so $\lvert\det\rvert = 1$ and
$R\,\mathcal{N}(0, I_N) = \mathcal{N}(0, R R^{\top}) = \mathcal{N}(0, I_N)$,
giving (i) and (ii). The likelihood is a function of $b_{\mathrm{std}}$
and $\theta$, whose joint prior is unchanged, so the posterior pushed
forward to the original coordinates is unchanged: (iii). (iv) follows from
$Q_{\cup}^{\top} Q_{\perp} = 0$. $\square$

`control$rotate_absorbable` is the case $\mathcal{C}$ = all columns: the
sampled coordinates are $U = Q_{\cup}^{\top} b_{\mathrm{std}}$ (the
`[k, q]` site `b_gen_U`) and $V = Q_{\perp}^{\top} b_{\mathrm{std}}$ (the
`[N - k, q]` site `b_gen_V`). `b_std` is recovered deterministically, and
everything downstream of it is untouched. Because the rotation acts on the
standardized draws, Proposition 6 makes the calibration of every estimand
identical to the unrotated fit's; Section 6.3 confirms this empirically.

*Remark (what is rotated, and on which side).* Two choices in
Proposition 6 are what make it safe, and both are easy to get wrong.
First, the rotation acts on the *sampled*, standardized coordinates
$b_{\mathrm{std}}$. Computing a rotated quantity from the draws after
sampling, as a deterministic transform, would leave the sampler's geometry
unchanged and could not affect mixing. Rotating the centered effects
$b$ instead would make the rotated prior covariance depend
on $\sigma_b$ and $\rho$, which reintroduces the funnel-type coupling that
the non-centred parameterization exists to remove. Second, the rotation
acts on the *subject* index, with the same $R$ for every column:
$\operatorname{vec}(b_{\mathrm{std}}) \mapsto (I_q \otimes R)\,
\operatorname{vec}(b_{\mathrm{std}})$. Because $L$ acts on the column
index, the two commute, $R^{\top} b = (R^{\top}
b_{\mathrm{std}})\, L^{\top}$. So the variance components enter exactly as
before, and the prior on the rotated coordinates is still independent
standard normal, $(I_q \otimes R)^{\top}(I_q \otimes R) = I$, for every
value of $\sigma_b$ and $\rho$. A generic rotation of the concatenated
$Nq$-vector, built to align particular combinations of intercept and slope
directions with the first coordinate axes, is also exact when applied to
$b_{\mathrm{std}}$. But such combinations, expressed in $b_{\mathrm{std}}$
coordinates, depend on $L$, so a fixed rotation of that kind aligns them
only at one value of $\rho$. Rotating each column by the same $Q_{\cup}$
aligns the whole span, which does not depend on $L$ (Section 5.2).

### 5.2 Where the degeneracy goes, and the dense block

Proposition 6 says the rotation is harmless. This subsection says what it
is for. The results come in two grades. Lemma 1 is exact for the full joint
model. Proposition 7 analyses the geometry that results, in a reduced
two-coordinate model with the variance components held fixed. Its
predictions are then checked in the closed-form model of
`dev/theory_rotation_toy.py` (Part 5) and against Section 6's fits.

**Lemma 1 (localization).** Let $(d, \Delta)$ be an invariant shift
(Definition 1), and write $\Delta = \Delta(d) + \Delta_0$, where
$\Delta_0$ has rows in the $K_i$ (a null shift). In the sampled
coordinates, the likelihood-invariant shift
$(\beta, B) \mapsto (\beta + c\,d,\; B + c\,\Delta(d))$ is

$$\beta \mapsto \beta + c\,d, \qquad
U \mapsto U + c\,Q_{\cup}^{\top} \Delta(d)\, (L^{\top})^{-1}, \qquad
V \mapsto V,$$

for every value of $\sigma_b$ and $L_{\mathrm{corr}}$. So every invariant
shift is a move in the coordinate block $(\beta, U)$, of dimension
$p + kq$, plus a null shift, which involves no fixed effect and moves only
coordinates the likelihood does not see. Without the rotation, the same
moves have a component on every one of the $N$ subjects' coordinates.

*Proof.* $B = b_{\mathrm{std}} L^{\top}$, so adding $c\,\Delta(d)$ to $B$
adds $c\,\Delta(d) (L^{\top})^{-1}$ to $b_{\mathrm{std}}$. Every column of
that is a combination of the columns of $\Delta(d)$, which lie in
$\mathcal{A} = \operatorname{span}(Q_{\cup})$, and
$Q_{\perp}^{\top} Q_{\cup} = 0$, so the $V$ coordinates do not move.
Invariance of the likelihood is Corollary 1. $\square$

Example 2 of Section 4.5 shows why the joint definition matters here: its
shift moves the intercept and slope columns together, along $x$. A basis
built column by column omits $x$, so that shift keeps a component outside
the block, on every subject's coordinates.

Lemma 1 is why the rotation acts on every column with the same $Q_{\cup}$.
The flat directions mix intercept and slope columns in proportions set by
the *sampled* $L$ (the $(L^{\top})^{-1}$ factor), but they always stay inside
the fixed block. A rotation of the intercept column alone captures them
only when $\rho = 0$.

Being flat in the likelihood is not the same as being flat in the
posterior. Along each invariant direction the priors on `beta` and on
`b_std` still pin the split, at scale $\sigma_b/\sqrt{N}$ on the `beta`
side (Section 3.2). What the rotation does is make the resulting ridge
between `beta` and $U$ a ridge between a *few named coordinates*, which a
small dense mass block can then absorb.

**Proposition 7 (the ridge, and what the dense block does).** Consider one
invariant direction, in the reduced model that holds every other coordinate
fixed. The statement is exact as written for the random intercept's mean
direction, whose witness is a single `beta` coordinate; for the other
generators the witness mixes several `beta` coordinates, and (ii) then
describes the whole $(\beta, U)$ block rather than one plane, with the
same conclusion about the dense block. Let $\tilde\beta$ be the coordinate of `beta` along the witness $d$,
with a diffuse prior, and $u$ the matching coordinate of $U$, with prior
$\mathcal{N}(0,1)$. Suppose the likelihood informs only the combination
$s = \tilde\beta + \kappa u$, with precision $\tau$. Then:

(i) $\operatorname{corr}(\tilde\beta, u \mid y) = -\big(1 + 1/(\tau\kappa^{2})\big)^{-1/2}$;

(ii) under a diagonal metric the plane's whitened covariance has
eigenvalues $1 \pm \lvert r\rvert$. It is therefore never *slow* (at most 2),
but it has a *narrow* direction of variance
$1 - \lvert r\rvert \approx 1/(2\tau\kappa^{2})$, which caps NUTS's step size;

(iii) with a dense block over $(\tilde\beta, u)$ the plane is exactly
whitened (both eigenvalues 1);

(iv) $\tau\kappa^{2}$ is a per-subject information ratio. For the random
intercept's mean direction, $\kappa = \sigma_0/\sqrt{N}$ and
$\tau = \sum_i n_i/\sigma_e^{2}$, so $\tau\kappa^{2} = \bar n\,\sigma_0^{2}/\sigma_e^{2}$.
This does not depend on $N$.

*Proof.* With a flat prior on $\tilde\beta$ the posterior precision of
$(\tilde\beta, u)$ is $\tau\,(1, \kappa)^{\top}(1, \kappa) +
\operatorname{diag}(0, 1)$. Its inverse is
$\tau^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} 1 + \tau\kappa^{2} & -\tau\kappa \\ -\tau\kappa & \tau
\end{pmatrix}$, which gives (i). (ii) holds because whitening a 2 x 2
covariance by its diagonal gives its correlation matrix. (iii) is the
definition of a dense metric block. For (iv), shifting the mean
direction of the intercepts by $u$ moves every subject's level by
$\sigma_0 u/\sqrt{N}$, and the data inform that common shift with
precision $\sum_i n_i/\sigma_e^{2}$. $\square$

So under a diagonal metric the rotation alone trades a slow direction for a
narrow one, and the narrow one gets worse exactly where the degeneracy is
worst: many visits per subject, or small noise. The dense block removes
it. The block is small ($p + kq$ coordinates: 10 in Section 6's design),
so it costs almost nothing per gradient. In the full closed-form posterior
(`dev/theory_rotation_toy.py`, Part 5(b); variance components fixed), the dense block cuts the whitened condition number by factors of 5 to 70, for
example from 12,037 to 174 with 8-20 visits per subject. What remains is
conditioning any fit has, such as the within-subject correlation between
intercept and slope. Part 5(a) checks (i) to six decimals.

**What a fixed dense block cannot do.** The ridge's orientation depends on
the *sampled* $L$ (Lemma 1): on $\sigma_0$ through $\kappa \propto \sigma_0$,
and, for directions shared between the intercept and slope columns, on
$\rho$ through $\rho/\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}$. NUTS adapts one fixed metric. The
$\sigma_0$ part is analysed here; the $\rho$ part is not, and it grows as
$\lvert\rho\rvert \to 1$. Let $\nu$ be the posterior coefficient of variation of
$\sigma_0$, roughly $1/\sqrt{2N}$. A metric that exactly whitens the plane
at one value of $\sigma_0$ leaves a residual condition number of
$1 + O\big(\nu\sqrt{\tau\kappa^{2}}\big)$ elsewhere in the posterior. In
units of the design, that is $1 + O\big(\sqrt{\bar n\,\sigma_0^{2}/(\sigma_e^{2}N)}\big)$:
small when there are many subjects relative to the information each one
carries, which is the usual regime for joint-model data. Part 5(c)
computes it directly:

| visits per subject | $N = 150$ | $N = 300$ | $N = 600$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2-11 | 1.76 | 1.50 | 1.31 |
| 8-20 | 2.71 | 2.05 | 1.64 |

The retired sweep has no such term. It removes the invariant directions
from the likelihood's coordinates exactly, for every value of $L$, at the
price of a correction step (development record, Sections 4.9-4.10). So the
no-sweep construction should lose some ground to the swept-and-rotated one
where the per-subject information is high or $N$ is small, and match it
otherwise. Section 6's grid ran both. Measured against two swept
comparators - with a diagonal metric, and with its own dense block - the
evidence is as follows.

- *Visits per subject: supported.* At $N = 300$, the no-sweep
  construction's ESS/sec relative to the swept one averaged 0.88x
  (diagonal comparator) and 0.90x (dense comparator) with about 17 visits
  per subject, against 0.99x and 1.18x with about 9. The stress grid
  (Section 6.4) extends this to about 35 visits, where it falls to
  0.51x-0.74x against the diagonal comparator.
- *$N$: supported once the information per subject is high.* In the core
  grid, with about 9 visits, the evidence was mixed. Against the diagonal
  comparator the ratios rise from $N = 150$ to $N = 300$ (0.73x/0.78x to
  1.05x/1.02x, intercept/slope), but against the dense comparator they do
  not (0.94x/1.13x at $N = 150$). $N = 600$ is not higher than $N = 300$
  for the intercept (0.93x against the diagonal comparator). With about 35
  visits, all four stress-grid pairs move the predicted way from
  $N = 50$ to $N = 100$: intercept 0.55x to 0.74x and slope 0.51x to 0.68x
  at $\rho = 0.3$; intercept 0.62x to 0.66x and slope 0.56x to 0.69x at
  $\rho = 0.95$.
- *$\rho$: no loss detected.* The argument above does not cover $\rho$,
  and the stress grid finds no consistent effect of raising it from 0.3
  to 0.95 at fixed visits and $N$.
- *Seed noise.* Per-seed ratios span 0.63x-1.85x in the core grid, wider
  than its effects, so three seeds settle only the larger stress-grid
  effects.

In short, the construction is within noise of the swept one in the
ordinary regime. It loses ground to the swept one as the information per
subject rises relative to $N$, as predicted, and is about half as
efficient in the most extreme stress cells. Against the unrotated fit it
is still 5x-30x ahead there (Section 6.4). A metric that follows the
sampled $\sigma_0$ is the obvious way to recover the difference, and has
not been tried.

### 5.3 Using it

The rotation and its dense block are on by default for NUTS fits
(`random_effects_method = "nuts"`) with either a random intercept only
($q = 1$), or a random intercept and slope ($q = 2$) with
`random_effects_corr = TRUE`, as long as no
legacy sweep option is requested. Elsewhere they are silently off.
`control = list(rotate_absorbable = FALSE)` gives the unrotated fit.
Setting `rotate_absorbable = TRUE` explicitly insists on the rotation and
raises an error outside that scope. What was rotated is reported in
`fit$convergence$orthogonalize$rotation` (`mode`, `applied`, `k`, and the
construction's diagnostics of Section 4.8).

**Random intercept only ($q = 1$).** For $q = 1$, `jmjax` samples $b$ directly, not non-centred, so the
rotation acts on $b$ itself. Its prior is iid $N(0, \sigma_b^{2})$, so the
rotated coordinates have the same prior for every $\sigma_b$, and
Proposition 6 holds unchanged. The ridge between `beta` and the rotated
block does not involve $\sigma_b$ in these centred coordinates. That removes
the fixed-metric residual of Section 5.2 for this case.

A random-intercept-only fit of `aids` and `pbc2` with the other settings
of Section 7 (`dev/pilot_q1_intercept.R`, unrotated) shows the
degeneracy clearly:

- `beta_0` and the subject-constant coefficients mixed at 0.04-0.07 ESS
  per draw, and 91%-95% of their posterior variance was explained by the
  absorbable directions of $b$;
- every other parameter was near 1 ESS per draw, with that share near 0.

The rotated arm of the same script, 2 seeds per dataset (ESS/sec
ratios, rotated over unrotated), shows:

| | `aids` | `pbc2` |
|---|---:|---:|
| `beta_0` and subject-constant coefficients | 51x-53x | 19x-20x |
| other parameters | 2.0x-3.5x | 0.56x-0.73x |
| `alpha` | 3.5x | 0.73x |
| slowest parameter, ESS per draw (unrotated, then rotated) | 0.05, 0.88 | 0.06, 0.78 |
| leapfrog steps per iteration (unrotated, then rotated) | 66, 29 | 31, 26 |

- **The affected coefficients.** They go from about one effective draw in
  17 to more than one per draw.
- **The other parameters.** On `aids` the rotation also removed the ridge
  that set the step size, so they gain too, as on the $q = 2$ `aids` fit
  (Section 7). On `pbc2` they lose some ESS/sec, but this is a loss of
  antithetic efficiency rather than of mixing. Unrotated they ran at
  1.3-1.6 ESS per draw; rotated, at 0.78-1.23. The pattern is the same
  as $q = 2$ on `pbc2`.
- **The fit as a whole.** What sets the chain length a user needs is the
  slowest parameter. On that measure, per draw, the rotation is about 17x
  better on `aids` and 12x better on `pbc2`.

The simulation grid confirms this (`dev/pilot_rotate_grid.R` with
`ROT_GRID=q1`: data with a random intercept only, 7 designs, 3 seeds,
2 chains of 1000 draws).

| visits/subject | $n$ | $\sigma_e$ | intercept | `age` | time slope | `alpha` |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 9 | 100 | 0.3 | 41x | 34x | 1.3x | 1.5x |
| 9 | 300 | 0.3 | 129x | 98x | 1.5x | 3.3x |
| 9 | 300 | 0.8 | 6.5x | 6.6x | 0.79x | 0.80x |
| 17 | 100 | 0.3 | 55x | 58x | 2.1x | 2.4x |
| 17 | 300 | 0.3 | 100x | 98x | 1.1x | 2.0x |
| 34 | 100 | 0.3 | 92x | 68x | 3.4x | 3.7x |
| 34 | 300 | 0.3 | 282x | 207x | 1.3x | 2.6x |

(ESS/sec, rotated over unrotated, geometric mean over seeds; `age` is the
subject-constant covariate.)

- **The unrotated fit often had not converged.** In 17 of the 21
  unrotated fits some parameter had R-hat above 1.05. The intercept's own
  R-hat reached 1.27, and it mixed at 0.002-0.04 ESS per draw everywhere
  except the noisy $\sigma_e = 0.8$ cell. Every rotated fit had R-hat at
  most 1.004. The large ratios therefore compare a converged fit with one
  that had not converged at this run length. Their exact size is not
  meaningful, but the order of magnitude is.
- **The pattern follows the theory.** The intercept and `age` gain
  together, and most with dense follow-up and low noise, where each
  subject pins its own level most tightly. The time slope has no
  absorbable direction at $q = 1$, so it moves only through the step size
  (0.79x-3.4x). `alpha` gains in six of the seven designs.
- **Exactness.** Posterior means agreed with the unrotated fit's to a
  median of 0.025 posterior SDs (maximum 0.175).

## 6. Simulation results

### 6.1 Design

`dev/pilot_rotate_grid.R` simulates from `dev/sim_joint.R`: a random
intercept and slope, with `y ~ time + age + sex`, `Surv(time, event) ~ trt`,
`sigma_b = (0.8, 0.3)`, `sigma_e = 0.3` and a spline baseline hazard. It
crosses visits per subject (about 9 against about 17), the generating
intercept-slope correlation $\rho \in \{0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9\}$ and, at
$\rho = 0.3$, $n \in \{150, 300, 600\}$: 10 cells, 3 seeds each, 500
warmup and 1000 draws on each of 2 chains. It compares an unrotated fit (`A`)
with the rotation plus its dense block (`A_rotdense`) on the same
simulated data. Both report the ordinary `beta`.

### 6.2 Efficiency

ESS/sec, averaged over seeds, for the two regression coefficients the
degeneracy affects most. The ratio is the geometric mean of the three
paired per-seed ratios.

| visits/subject | $\rho$ | $n$ | intercept: unrotated | rotated | ratio | time slope: unrotated | rotated | ratio | `alpha` ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| ~9 | 0.0 | 300 | 25.9 | 354.4 | 14.2x | 9.1 | 304.9 | 36.4x | 0.85x |
| ~17 | 0.0 | 300 | 12.1 | 229.4 | 19.3x | 4.0 | 234.9 | 59.2x | 1.32x |
| ~9 | 0.3 | 300 | 30.0 | 253.3 | 8.6x | 19.0 | 251.1 | 13.4x | 0.72x |
| ~17 | 0.3 | 300 | 11.3 | 248.5 | 22.2x | 6.4 | 262.5 | 41.9x | 1.33x |
| ~9 | 0.6 | 300 | 26.1 | 245.7 | 9.4x | 29.9 | 229.3 | 7.7x | 1.00x |
| ~17 | 0.6 | 300 | 9.6 | 231.6 | 24.0x | 10.0 | 251.2 | 24.9x | 1.59x |
| ~9 | 0.9 | 300 | 20.4 | 220.7 | 11.1x | 20.3 | 250.3 | 12.8x | 0.90x |
| ~17 | 0.9 | 300 | 8.9 | 218.9 | 24.9x | 8.6 | 217.7 | 25.6x | 1.59x |
| ~9 | 0.3 | 150 | 41.8 | 323.7 | 7.6x | 32.6 | 420.4 | 13.1x | 0.76x |
| ~9 | 0.3 | 600 | 15.9 | 132.0 | 8.2x | 8.8 | 151.7 | 17.7x | 0.77x |

Across all 30 paired fits the geometric-mean gain is 13.5x for the
intercept (per-seed range 4.5x-31.6x) and 21.1x for the time slope
(5.1x-70.8x). Wall time is essentially unchanged (1.03x; 0.83x-1.10x), so
the gain is almost entirely ESS per draw. The median ESS over 2000 draws is
about 3,450 for both coefficients under the rotation - more than the
number of draws, the anti-correlated sampling NUTS achieves on a
well-conditioned target - against 180-235 for the unrotated fit. The
association parameter `alpha`, which the degeneracy does not involve, is
not unchanged: its ratio splits by design. It is 0.72x-1.00x in all six
cells with about 9 visits per subject and 1.32x-1.59x in all four with
about 17 (geometric mean 1.04x overall). Why the rotation helps `alpha`
with dense follow-up and costs it a little otherwise is not yet
understood. There
were no divergences, and the worst R-hat on a reported coefficient was
1.002 under the rotation, against 1.044 for the unrotated fit.

The pattern follows the mechanism. The gain is largest where each subject
carries the most information about its own random effects (the
dense-visit cells: 19x-25x and 25x-59x). There the prior pins the split
between `beta` and the absorbable directions least, relative to how
tightly the data pin each subject. The gain does not grow with $n$ (8.2x
at $n = 600$ against 7.6x at $n = 150$), as expected: the degeneracy's
geometry is set by per-subject information, not by the number of
subjects.

### 6.3 Calibration

The rotation cannot change the posterior (Proposition 6), so this checks
the implementation. `dev/study_calibration.R`, `linear` design,
$n = 300$, $R = 100$ replicates, gated on regression-parameter
R-hat $\le 1.05$ (all 100 kept):

| estimand | unrotated: cov95 | sd_ratio | bias/se | rotated: cov95 | sd_ratio | bias/se |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `beta_0` | 0.99 | 1.164 | 1.68 | 0.99 | 1.150 | 1.55 |
| `beta_slope` | 0.97 | 1.027 | -0.30 | 0.96 | 1.038 | -0.32 |
| `alpha` | 0.93 | 0.922 | 2.97 | 0.93 | 0.917 | 2.97 |
| `sigma_b0` | 0.94 | 0.914 | 0.63 | 0.95 | 0.906 | 0.68 |

Coverage agrees to within 0.01 everywhere (the Monte Carlo SE of a 95%
coverage estimate from 100 replicates is about 0.022), and the ratio of mean posterior SD to the SD of
posterior means to within 0.015 - agreement within Monte Carlo error. The two effects visible in *both* columns -
slightly wide intervals for `beta_0`, and an upward bias in `alpha` of
about 3 Monte Carlo SEs - belong to the model and this design, not to the
rotation. Section 9 traces the second to ordinary finite-sample bias that
shrinks with $n$.

The retired sweep, with its correction and the same rotation, reached
similar efficiency (the no-sweep construction averaged about 0.92x of it
in the same grid; Section 5.2) and the same calibration. The side-by-side
numbers are in the development record's Epilogue.

### 6.4 Stress grid

Section 5.2 names two regimes where the rotation should be weakest. One
is few subjects, each carrying a lot of information, where a fixed metric
cannot follow the ridge's dependence on the sampled $\sigma_0$. The other
is strongly correlated random effects, which that argument does not
cover. `dev/pilot_rotate_grid.R` with `ROT_GRID=stress` targets both. It
runs six cells:

- about 35 visits per subject, crossed with $N \in \{50, 100\}$ and
  $\rho \in \{0.3, 0.95\}$;
- $\rho = 0.95$ at about 9 visits ($N = 100$);
- $\rho = 0.95$ at about 17 visits ($N = 300$).

Each cell has 3 seeds, and each fit is compared with the unrotated fit and
with the retired sweep-and-rotation (diagonal metric) on the same data.

The criterion fixed before the run was that the rotation must not fall
below the unrotated fit's ESS/sec on the reported coefficients in any
cell. It did not. The lowest cell was 5.5x and the lowest single seed
3.2x.

| visits | $N$ | $\rho$ | intercept vs unrotated | slope vs unrotated | `alpha` vs unrotated | intercept vs sweep | slope vs sweep |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 35 | 50 | 0.30 | 5.5x | 10.3x | 1.60x | 0.55x | 0.51x |
| 35 | 50 | 0.95 | 21.1x | 21.6x | 2.42x | 0.62x | 0.56x |
| 35 | 100 | 0.30 | 14.5x | 27.1x | 1.58x | 0.74x | 0.68x |
| 35 | 100 | 0.95 | 26.0x | 28.6x | 1.73x | 0.66x | 0.69x |
| 9 | 100 | 0.95 | 7.0x | 7.5x | 0.74x | 1.02x | 0.88x |
| 17 | 300 | 0.95 | 24.6x | 29.7x | 1.09x | 0.77x | 0.83x |

(ESS/sec ratios, geometric means over 3 seeds.)

The rotated fit's posterior means agreed with the unrotated fit's to a
median of 0.029 posterior SDs (maximum 0.166, 90 pairs). There were no
divergences, and the worst R-hat over all monitored parameters was 1.046
(1.043 for the unrotated fit). Wall time was 0.86x-1.06x the unrotated
fit's.

The table bears out three points.

- **The weak spot is weak only against the retired sweep.** The
  predicted weakness shows up as a loss relative to the sweep, not
  relative to the unrotated fit. The cell with the fewest subjects and
  lowest $\rho$ gains least over the unrotated fit (5.5x), and it is also
  where the sweep leads by most (about 2x). This is Section 5.2's
  $1 + O\big(\sqrt{\bar n\,\sigma_0^{2}/(\sigma_e^{2}N)}\big)$ residual in
  action.
- **Strong correlation between the random effects did not hurt.** At
  $\rho = 0.95$ the gains over the unrotated fit are as large as, or larger
  than, at $\rho = 0.3$, because the unrotated fit degrades faster.
- **`alpha` repeats Section 6.2's split by visits.** It fell to 0.74x
  with about 9 visits. It rose to 1.09x with about 17 and to 1.58x-2.42x
  with about 35.

## 7. Real data

`dev/study_realdata_rotate.R` fits two standard joint-model datasets
(bundled with `JMbayes2`) twice from the same `lme()`/`coxph()` pre-fit
and the same sampler seed. One fit is unrotated; the other uses
`rotate_absorbable` with `dense_mass_generator_beta`. Each has 4 chains of
1000 warmup and 1000 draws, and there are 3 seeds per dataset.

- **`aids`** (Guo & Carlin 2004; 467 patients): `sqrt(CD4) ~ obstime +
  drug + gender`, random intercept and slope on `obstime`,
  `Surv(Time, death) ~ drug`. It played no part in finding the
  degeneracy. There are three absorbable intercept directions (constant,
  `drug`, `gender`) and one slope direction.
- **`pbc2`** (312 patients): `log(serBilir) ~ year + age`, random
  intercept and slope on `year`, `Surv(years, death) ~ drug`. This is the
  dataset on which the degeneracy was first measured (Section 3.5). There
  are two absorbable intercept directions (constant, `age`) and one slope
  direction.

ESS/sec ratios are means over seeds, rotated over unrotated; the per-seed
range is in brackets:

| parameter | `aids` | `pbc2` |
|---|---:|---:|
| intercept | 26.9x [21-34] | 17.2x [12-25] |
| time slope | 2.3x [2.0-2.7] | 4.4x [4.0-4.6] |
| subject-constant covariates | 24.8x, 28.5x (`drug`, `gender`) [21-33] | 16.6x (`age`) [12-23] |
| `alpha` | 2.0x [1.8-2.4] | 0.95x [0.88-1.01] |
| `sigma_e`, `sigma_b`, `rho`, `gamma` | 1.4x-2.4x | 0.82x-1.28x |
| NUTS sampling time | 10.8 s against 17.6 s | 12.4 s against 11.7 s |
| mean leapfrog steps per iteration | 31 against 92-111 | 60-63 against 63 |
| max R-hat, all parameters | 1.010 against 1.010 | 1.007 against 1.018 |

The pattern is the one the theory predicts. The coefficients on the
absorbable directions - the intercept and the subject-constant covariates -
gain 17x-28x (12x-34x across seeds), the time slope 2.3x-4.4x. As for the exactness check: every
posterior mean agrees between the two fits within Monte Carlo error
(largest paired difference 1.65 Monte Carlo SEs over the 19
parameter-dataset pairs; the rotation cannot change the posterior,
Proposition 6).

The two datasets differ in one instructive way. On `aids`, the unrotated
fit's trajectories were three times longer (92-111 leapfrog steps against
31): the degeneracy was what set NUTS's trajectory length. Removing it cut
the cost of every iteration, so *every* parameter gained, `alpha` included
(2.0x), and total sampling time fell by 40%. On `pbc2` the trajectory
length was set by something else (63 steps in both fits). There the
parameters the degeneracy does not involve are unchanged or slightly slower
(`sigma_e` 0.82x, `gamma_0` 0.85x, `alpha` 0.95x), for 6% more time. The
same dependence on what sets the trajectory length is a plausible
reading of Section 6.2's `alpha` split, though it was not measured there.

For comparison: the retired sweep's reportable, corrected coefficients
gained roughly 1.3x in simulation (development record, Section 9.1.1),
and on `aids` the sweep moved `alpha` by 1.5x (Section 7.1 there). The
rotation gives an order of magnitude on the former and a little more on
the latter, with no correction step.

## 8. The comparison with JMbayes2

### 8.1 The association parameter: a generic NUTS advantage

The association parameter `alpha` is the primary inferential target of a
joint model (Section 1). The association between the marker and the
hazard is what the model is built to study; the other parameters are
largely there so that `alpha` is estimated correctly. The degeneracy of Section 3 does not
involve it; the rotation's effect on it is mixed (Section 6.2: 0.72x-1.59x by design, 1.04x overall). Measured
directly against `JMbayes2`, `jmjax`'s *unrotated* fit mixes `alpha` much
faster. In a replicated covariate-count sweep (`dev/study_orth_vs_jmbayes2.R`:
$n = 1000$, 3 seeds, `JMbayes2` at 16,000 iterations with 4,000 burn-in per
chain, well above its own defaults):

| k | unrotated `jmjax` vs `JMbayes2`, `alpha` ESS/sec |
|---:|---:|
| 1 | 5.72x |
| 4 | 8.07x |
| 8 | 6.22x |
| 12 | 6.25x |

On real data (`dev/study_common_ess.R`, the designs of Section 7,
3 seeds, `JMbayes2` at the same 16,000/4,000 iterations, and NumPyro's ESS
estimator for every fit), the unrotated fit's `alpha` ESS/sec was 3.5x
`JMbayes2`'s on `aids` and 8.2x on `pbc2`. This is the generic NUTS/HMC-versus-block-Gibbs distinction of
Sections 2.2 and 2.4 (Hoffman & Gelman 2014; Roberts & Sahu 1997; Betancourt
2017). A gradient-based sampler moves the whole parameter vector jointly.
It has no equivalent of "conditional on the other blocks' current values",
so growing inter-parameter correlation has no specific mechanism by which
to degrade one block's own updates. It is not a `jmjax`-specific
achievement, but it is the part of the comparison that needs no caveat,
and it is present with no option enabled.

**Why: a theoretical account.** The argument can be made precise. Write
$R$ for every parameter other than `alpha`: the random effects, `beta`,
`gamma`, the baseline hazard and the variance components.

> **Proposition 8 (blocked updates of `alpha`).** Consider the two-block
> sampler that draws `alpha` exactly from $p(\alpha \mid R, y)$ and then $R$
> exactly from $p(R \mid \alpha, y)$. At stationarity, the lag-1
> autocorrelation of its `alpha` chain is
> $$r \;=\; \frac{\operatorname{Var}(E[\alpha \mid R, y])}{\operatorname{Var}(\alpha \mid y)}
> \;=\; 1 - \frac{E[\operatorname{Var}(\alpha \mid R, y)]}{\operatorname{Var}(\alpha \mid y)},$$
> the fraction of `alpha`'s posterior variance explained by the other
> parameters (its "fraction of missing information"). If the posterior is
> Gaussian, $r$ is the squared multiple correlation $R^2$ of `alpha` on $R$.
> The `alpha` chain is then exactly AR(1) with coefficient $R^2$, so its
> integrated autocorrelation time is $(1+R^2)/(1-R^2)$ and its ESS per draw
> is $(1-R^2)/(1+R^2)$.

*Proof.* The `alpha` chain of a two-block sampler is a data-augmentation
chain. Its lag-1 autocovariance is $\operatorname{Var}(E[\alpha \mid R])$
(Liu, Wong & Kong 1994), which gives the first expression; the second
follows from the law of total variance. In the Gaussian case,
$E[\alpha \mid R]$ is linear in $R$ and $E[R \mid \alpha]$ is linear in
$\alpha$. Composing the two regressions gives
$\alpha_{t+1} = c + R^2 \alpha_t + \varepsilon_t$ with $\varepsilon_t$
independent of the past, because the coefficient is
$\operatorname{Cov}(\alpha,R)\Sigma_R^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(R,\alpha)/\operatorname{Var}(\alpha) = R^2$. $\square$

The two-block sampler is a benchmark, not a model of `JMbayes2`.
`JMbayes2` splits $R$ into several blocks and updates `alpha` and the
coefficients with adaptive random-walk Metropolis rather than exact
conditional draws. Both changes can generally be expected to make it
slower still (Liu, Wong & Kong 1994; Roberts & Sahu 1997), although
neither is guaranteed to in every case.

Two sources make $R^2$ large in a joint model. The first is errors in
variables. Given the random effects, the marker trajectory
$m_i(t) = x_i(t)^{\top}\beta + z_i(t)^{\top} b_i$ is known exactly, and
`alpha` is just the coefficient on a known time-varying covariate in a
survival model. That is sharp. Marginally, `alpha` also carries the
uncertainty in every trajectory, and the better the other parameters
predict it, the more of its variance is "missing" given them. The second
is the hazard's own location. Changing the level of $m_i(t)$ across all
subjects changes $\alpha\,m_i(t)$ by a constant that the log baseline
hazard absorbs. So `alpha` is correlated with the baseline-hazard level
unless the marker is centred. `dev/alpha_missing_information.R` estimates
$R^2$ from a long rotated fit (4 chains of 5,000 draws) and splits it
between these two sources. The second dominates. On `aids`, the survival
block alone (`gamma` and the baseline-hazard coefficients) explains 0.86
of `alpha`'s posterior variance, and the random effects alone explain
0.30. On `pbc2` the figures are 0.82 and 0.20. The errors-in-variables
part is real, but most of what a blocked sampler conditions away is the
trade-off between `alpha` and the level of the log hazard.

HMC is not a blocked sampler. It moves `alpha` and $R$ together along the
gradient, so a correlation between them is simply part of the posterior's
shape. Under a fixed metric, the cost of that shape is paid in leapfrog
steps per iteration, which scale with the ratio of the longest to the
shortest posterior scale, $\sqrt{\kappa}$ (Neal 2011). The
autocorrelation per iteration is not affected. A single correlation of
`alpha` with $R$ at $R^2$ contributes
$\kappa = (1+\sqrt{R^2})/(1-\sqrt{R^2})$, so $\sqrt{\kappa}$ grows like
$1/\sqrt{1-R^2}$, against $1/(1-R^2)$ for the blocked sampler. There is also
a second, larger effect. In a joint model the step size is usually set
already by some other narrow direction (the spline coefficients, the
variance components, or the Section 3 ridge in an unrotated fit). While
`alpha`'s correlation is not the narrowest direction, it adds nothing
to the step count at all. A blocked sampler pays $(1+R^2)/(1-R^2)$
regardless.

`dev/theory_alpha_toy.py` checks this on a Gaussian target, using the
stylised exact-dynamics HMC model of `dev/theory_rotation_toy.py`. The
simulated two-block Gibbs lag-1 autocorrelation equals $R^2$ to within
0.004 at every value tried. Its integrated autocorrelation time goes
3.0, 9.0, 27.6, 39.0 and 199 as $R^2$ goes 0.5, 0.8, 0.93, 0.95 and 0.99.
The HMC model's `alpha` IAT stays between 1.6 and 2.1. The gradients it
needs per independent draw go 4.8, 9.4, 17.1, 20.5 and 46.8. With an
unrelated ridge at correlation 0.995 already in $R$, its step count is
22.2 at every $R^2$ from 0 to 0.99.

The real-data measurements have the shape Proposition 8 predicts.
`JMbayes2` is the cheaper sampler per draw; the gap is in what each draw
is worth.

| | `aids` | `pbc2` |
|---|---:|---:|
| `JMbayes2`: draws/sec | 1726 | 2390 |
| `JMbayes2`: `alpha` ESS per draw | 0.032 | 0.025 |
| `jmjax` rotated: draws/sec | 373 | 327 |
| `jmjax` rotated: `alpha` ESS per draw | 1.06 | 1.46 |
| ESS-per-draw ratio x draws/sec ratio | 33.3 x 0.216 = 7.2 | 57.8 x 0.137 = 7.9 |

(`dev/study_common_ess.R`, 3 seeds, NumPyro's estimator for both
packages, geometric means; the last row is the `alpha` ESS/sec of
Section 8.3. `JMbayes2`'s own estimator gives it 0.035 and 0.028 ESS per
draw.) `JMbayes2` draws 4.6-7.3 times faster but keeps only one effective
draw in 31-40. Under Proposition 8, an ESS per draw of 0.025-0.032
corresponds to $R^2 \approx 0.94$-$0.95$ for an ideal two-block sampler. `jmjax`'s ESS
per draw on `alpha` is at or above 1 on both datasets, as the HMC argument
predicts.

The same script measures that $R^2$ directly, with 960 regressors on
`aids` and 649 on `pbc2`, adjusted for their number:

| | `aids` | `pbc2` |
|---|---:|---:|
| $R^2$(`alpha` given everything else) | 0.873 | 0.853 |
| ideal two-block sampler, predicted ESS per draw | 0.068 | 0.079 |
| `JMbayes2`, measured ESS per draw | 0.032 | 0.025 |
| `jmjax` NUTS, measured ESS per draw (same long fit) | 1.05 | 1.72 |

So `alpha` shares 85%-87% of its posterior variance with the other
parameters. Even an ideal blocked sampler, drawing exactly from each full
conditional, would keep only one effective draw in 13-15.
`JMbayes2` does 2-3 times worse than that ideal. That is the direction
expected from its random-walk Metropolis steps and finer blocking.

The linear $R^2$ is also a lower bound on the fraction in Proposition 8:
the best linear predictor of `alpha` explains no more of its variance than
$E[\alpha \mid R, y]$ does. So the true ideal benchmark can only be worse than
the table's, and the 2-3x remainder is an upper bound on what
`JMbayes2`'s implementation adds.

On a log scale, the ideal benchmark is 78% of the measured ESS-per-draw
gap between `jmjax` and `JMbayes2` on `aids` (15.4x of 33x) and 73% on
`pbc2` (21.7x of 68x). This is a descriptive comparison of different
transition kernels, not a causal decomposition: it says that the
dependence of `alpha` on the other parameters is large enough to account
for most of the gap, not how the remainder divides among implementation
choices. Any sampler that updates `alpha`
conditional on the survival parameters inherits it. A gradient sampler
that moves them together does not.

The same measurements show what a blocked sampler would need to escape
this. Suppose `alpha`, `gamma` and the baseline-hazard coefficients were
updated together as one block, and the random effects as the other.
Proposition 8 then applies with $R$ the random effects alone. Their
$R^2$ is 0.30 on `aids` and 0.20 on `pbc2`, which gives an ideal ESS per
draw of about 0.54 and 0.67 instead of 0.07-0.08. But that block has
10-20 strongly correlated dimensions, and exact draws from it are not
available. An adaptive random-walk proposal on a block that size and
that correlated is itself slow. NUTS gets the joint move without any
block design or proposal tuning. That is the sense in which the
advantage is intrinsic to it.

Proposition 8 also explains one result in Section 7. On `aids`, the
rotation raised `alpha`'s ESS/sec 2x without touching `alpha`'s
geometry: it removed the ridge that set the step size (92-111 leapfrog
steps down to 31), and `alpha` rides on whatever sets the step count.

### 8.2 JMbayes2's own degradation with k

Independently of anything about `jmjax`, `JMbayes2`'s random-effects
covariance parameter (`D.D[...]`, a fixed 2x2 block regardless of `k`)
shows a clear, replicated collapse in R-hat as `k` grows:

| k | JMbayes2 all-params max R-hat (seed range across replication) |
|---:|---|
| 1  | 1.008 |
| 4  | 1.072 |
| 8  | 191.8 - 329.7 |
| 12 | 6997.6 - 11087.7 |

confirmed consistent across all 3 replication seeds at both k=8 and k=12 (no
seed came close to converging at either point). This is the block-Gibbs
correlation-growth mechanism described in Section 2.4 (Roberts & Sahu 1997):
nothing about the model's identifiability changes with `k` here (the
covariance block is always 2x2), but the *conditional* correlation the
Gibbs step has to move through grows as more absorbable fixed-effects
directions are added to the design - exactly the setting that literature
predicts degrades block/conditional samplers specifically. This is also
precisely why the naive "all-parameters ESS/sec, jmjax vs JMbayes2" ratio
would look enormous at k=12 (hundreds-fold, driven by `JMbayes2`'s R-hat of
11,000+) without being an honest measurement of anything - which is why
this document compares parameters a user reports, not the larger raw
number.

### 8.3 The regression coefficients: the rotation closes the one gap

On the regression coefficients, the unrotated fit was *behind* `JMbayes2`.
The location degeneracy of Section 3 is exactly the problem that
hierarchical centering - the centered parameterization of Section 2.1
(Gelfand, Sahu & Carlin 1995) - solves. `JMbayes2` hierarchically centres
the coefficients it can (its prior arguments distinguish "hierarchically
centered" coefficients from the rest; `?JMbayes2::jm`). `jmjax` keeps the
non-centred parameterization, which it needs for the random-effect
variances (Section 2.2), and until now paid for it on these coefficients.
The rotation removes that payment. ESS/sec relative to `JMbayes2`, same
data and settings as Section 7 (`dev/study_common_ess.R`: the draws of all
three fits saved, and every ESS computed with NumPyro's estimator;
geometric means over 3 seeds; `JMbayes2`'s time is its whole `jm()` call):

| parameter | `aids`: unrotated / `JMbayes2` | rotated / `JMbayes2` | `pbc2`: unrotated / `JMbayes2` | rotated / `JMbayes2` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| intercept | 0.04x | 0.97x | 0.05x | 0.93x |
| subject-constant covariates | 0.03x-0.04x | 0.88x-0.98x | 0.06x | 0.98x |
| time slope | 3.3x | 7.7x | 0.42x | 1.9x |
| `alpha` | 3.5x | 7.2x | 8.2x | 7.9x |
| survival coefficient `gamma` | 1.2x | 2.8x | 2.1x | 1.8x |

With the rank-normalized bulk ESS of the `posterior` package the ratios
are within 5% of these, and with each package's own estimator within 18%
(`JMbayes2`'s own estimator is somewhat more generous to it).

With the rotation, `jmjax` is at parity with `JMbayes2` (0.88x-0.98x) on
exactly the coefficients hierarchical centering is designed for. It is
ahead on everything else: the time slope (1.9x-7.7x), the survival
coefficient (1.8x-2.8x), and the association parameter (7.2x-7.9x). Before
the rotation, the unrotated fit trailed by a factor of 17-33 on the first
group (0.03x-0.06x).

### 8.4 Synthesis

Two effects should be reported separately. The comparison with `JMbayes2`
on `alpha` (Section 8.1) is large and generic, and needs no
reparameterization. The rotation (Sections 5-7) is specific to this model
class. It removes a cost that the non-centred parameterization pays on the
regression coefficients, which brings those coefficients from far behind
`JMbayes2` to parity with it (Section 8.3), without changing any reported
quantity.

## 9. Limitations and next steps

- **`alpha`'s small upward bias is ordinary finite-sample bias.** In the
  calibration study `alpha` sat $2.8\%$ above the truth at $n = 300$ in
  every arm, the unrotated fit included. Small-sample bias in the
  association parameter is a known feature of joint models, and $n = 300$
  is small. `dev/study_alpha_bias.R` confirms it:
  - neither the simulator's baseline-hazard calibration nor the spline
    baseline explains it (paired changes $-0.0016$ and $-0.0011$, SE about
