    $0.0025$);
  - at $n = 1200$ it falls to $1.1\%$, which is not significant ($1.7$
    Monte Carlo SEs), with coverage $0.92$ and $\mathrm{sd\_ratio}$
    $0.955$.
- **Scope.** The rotation is implemented under the default NUTS sampler
  for $q = 1$, and for $q = 2$ with correlated random effects (jmjax fits
  at most two random effects). Elsewhere the default
  leaves it off, and an explicit `rotate_absorbable = TRUE` raises an
  informative error. The simulation evidence is one design
  family (Section 6.1), with a spline baseline hazard; the earlier sweep
  pilots also covered a Weibull hazard.
- **Near-collinearity.** The basis construction's rank decision is a
  tolerance judgement when absorbable and identified directions are nearly
  collinear, although every returned direction is verified before use
  (Section 4.8).
- **Condition (S).** It can fail for very flexible time bases with few
  observations per subject. The fit then warns and leaves the failing
  directions out of the rotation (Section 4.8).
- **The construction behind the reported fits.** The fits in Sections 5-8
  used the 0.3.x construction, column by column. For those designs it gives
  the same subspace as the joint construction of Section 4 (Proposition 4),
  so no reported number depends on the change.
- **Known costs, left as they are.** Two small costs are recorded rather
  than tuned away. Neither stops a fit or biases it, and both were
  measured in simulation, not in real data.
  - With about 9 visits per subject, the rotation gives `alpha` 0.72x-1.00x
    of the unrotated fit's ESS/sec (Sections 6.2 and 6.4). It gains with
    denser follow-up, and on real data it was 2.0x (`aids`) and 0.95x
    (`pbc2`). The mechanism is not established, and `alpha` remains far
    ahead of `JMbayes2` either way (Section 8).
  - In the most information-dense stress designs, the retired sweep is up
    to about 2x more efficient than the rotation, as Section 5.2 predicts.
    The rotation is still 5x-30x ahead of the unrotated fit there.

  A metric that follows the sampled $\sigma_0$ could recover the second.
  Both will be revisited if users meet them in real data.
- **Next steps.** A metric that follows the sampled $\sigma_0$, for
  example by rescaling the dense block with the current $L$, is the obvious
  way to remove the residual of Section 5.2 and has not been tried. Broader
  design checks: more covariates, a non-linear time trend (Section 4.5's
  Example 1), a coupled design (Example 2) and the `mixing` design. The
  construction needs only the fixed- and random-effects designs, so it
  carries over to any model whose random effects enter through a linear
  predictor, including generalized linear mixed models; crossed random
  effects would need one basis per grouping factor, each rotating that
  factor's own index. More than two random effects per subject ($q \ge 3$)
  is not supported by `jmjax`'s fitting code, although the construction of
  Section 4 is (it is tested at $q = 3$).

## 10. Related work summary

Section 2 covers this in full. In brief, this document sits at the
intersection of:

- general non-centered/centered reparameterization theory for hierarchical
  models (Papaspiliopoulos & Roberts 2003; Papaspiliopoulos, Roberts &
  Sköld 2007);
- the geometric account of why this matters for Hamiltonian/NUTS samplers
  (Betancourt & Girolami 2013; Betancourt 2017; Hoffman & Gelman 2014;
  Neal 2003 for the related-but-distinct funnel case), and the analysis of
  linear preconditioning for HMC (Neal 2011; Hird & Livingstone 2025);
- the account of why block/Gibbs samplers are specifically vulnerable to
  growing correlation (Roberts & Sahu 1997);
- applied precedent for this failure mode (Ogle et al. 2020);
- the fact that effective sample size belongs to a functional, not a
  sampler (Geyer 1992).

The closest structural relative of the retired sweep is restricted spatial
regression (Reich, Hodges & Zadnik 2006; Hughes & Haran 2013; Hanks et
al. 2015; Khan & Calder 2022; Bradley 2024). The rotation differs in kind:
it restricts nothing.

## 11. Conclusion

`jmjax`'s joint model has a location degeneracy between fixed effects and
random effects. It recurs for the random slope whatever the covariate
count, and it slows an unrotated fit on exactly the coefficients a user
reports.

`jmjax` addresses it, by default, with a rotation and a small dense mass block. The
random effects are rotated so the absorbable directions become a small
explicit block, and that block and `beta` share one dense mass block. The
model, the prior and every reported quantity are unchanged (Proposition 6),
and calibration matches the unrotated fit (Section 6.3). The cost of the
degeneracy is removed: in simulation the intercept and time slope gain
14x and 21x in ESS/sec (geometric means), and on real data the intercept
and subject-constant covariates gain 17x-28x and the time slope
2.3x-4.4x, at similar or lower wall time. A stress grid aimed at the
theory's weak spots kept the gains at 5x-30x. For random-intercept-only
models the rotation turns fits that often had not converged at the
standard run length into ones that had (Section 5.3).

The theory (Section 5.2) says where the approach is weakest: few subjects
each carrying a lot of information, and strongly correlated random
effects. It also says why - a fixed mass matrix can only average over the
ridge's dependence on the sampled variance components.

With the rotation, `jmjax` matches `JMbayes2` on the coefficients
`JMbayes2` hierarchically centres, where the unrotated fit trailed by a
factor of 17-33. It is 1.8x-7.9x ahead on the rest (Section 8.3). That includes the
association parameter `alpha`, the quantity a joint model exists to
estimate, where the lead is 7.2x-7.9x. That advantage is generic to NUTS
and needs none of this. Proposition 8 accounts for it: a sampler that
updates `alpha` given the other parameters pays for their correlation
with `alpha` in autocorrelation, while HMC pays for it, if at all, in
integration steps. On real data, 85%-87% of `alpha`'s posterior
variance is shared with the other parameters, mostly the survival block.
That caps an ideal blocked sampler at one effective draw in 13-15, and it
explains about three quarters of the measured gap.
